blocks.prompt: 2 A town's population is modeled by \(P(t) = \dfrac{100{,}000}{1 + 9e^{-0.5t}}\). What is the long-term population as \(t \to \infty\)?
blocks.explanation:
A real-world limit at infinity (a logistic population model).
"Long-term population" means \(\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t)\).
Plan: find the limit of the denominator using \(e^{-0.5t} \to 0\), then divide.
steps:
Given: \(P(t) = \dfrac{100{,}000}{1 + 9e^{-0.5t}}\).
To find: \(\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t)\).
Method: Limit of a quotient = quotient of the limits (the denominator's limit is not 0).
Key fact: for a positive constant \(k\), as \(t \to \infty\), \(e^{kt} \to \infty\) and \(e^{-kt} = \dfrac{1}{e^{kt}} \to 0\) (Important Result: \(\lim_{x \to \infty} e^{x} = \infty\), \(\lim_{x \to -\infty} e^{x} = 0\)).

Limit of the exponential term
\[\lim_{t \to \infty} e^{-0.5t} = 0\]
\[\lim_{t \to \infty} 9e^{-0.5t} = 9 \times 0 = 0\]
Why: \(e^{-0.5t} = \frac{1}{e^{0.5t}}\) and \(e^{0.5t} \to \infty\).

Limit of the denominator
\[\lim_{t \to \infty} (1 + 9e^{-0.5t}) = 1 + 0 = 1\]
Why: Limit of a sum = sum of the limits.

Limit of \(P(t)\)
\[\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t) = \frac{100{,}000}{1}\]
\[= 100{,}000\]
Why: The denominator tends to 1, which is not 0, so the quotient rule applies.

Meaning and check
\[P(0) = \frac{100{,}000}{1 + 9} = 10{,}000\]
\[P(20) = \frac{100{,}000}{1 + 9e^{-10}} \approx 99{,}959\]
Why: The town starts at 10,000 people and grows towards 100,000 but never passes it: 100,000 is the long-term (carrying) level.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints "100,00010". This is a printing error: the long-term population is \(100{,}000\).
